What counts as small or large depends on the specific viewing conditions and follows from Ricco's law. In general, in order to adequately assess an object's visibility one needs to know both parameters. This is the reason the extreme naked eye limit for viewing a star is apparent magnitude 8, but only apparent magnitude 6.9 for galaxies.

Surface brightnesses are usually quoted in magnitudes per square arcsecond. Because the magnitude is logarithmic, calculating surface brightness cannot be done by simple division of magnitude by area. Instead, for a source with a total or integrated magnitude m extending over a visual area of A square arcseconds, the surface brightness S is given by {\displaystyle S=m+2.5\cdot \log _{10}A.} For astronomical objects, surface brightness is analogous to photometric luminance and is therefore constant with distance: as an object becomes fainter with distance, it also becomes correspondingly smaller in visual area. In geometrical terms, for a nearby object emitting a given amount of light, radiative flux decreases with the square of the distance to the object, but the physical area corresponding to a given solid angle or visual area (e.g. 1 square arcsecond) decreases by the same proportion, resulting in the same surface brightness. For extended objects such as nebulae or galaxies, this allows the estimation of spatial distance from surface brightness by means of the distance modulus or luminosity distance.

The surface brightness in magnitude units is related to the surface brightness in physical units of solar luminosity per square parsec by {\displaystyle S(\mathrm {mag/arcsec^{2}} )=M_{\odot }+21.572-2.5\log _{10}S(L_{\odot }/\mathrm {pc} ^{2}),} where {\displaystyle M_{\odot }} and {\displaystyle L_{\odot }} are the absolute magnitude and the luminosity of the Sun in chosen color-band respectively. Surface brightness can also be expressed in candela per square metre using the formula [value in cd/m2] = 10.8864×104 × 10(−0.4×[value in mag/arcsec2]).

A truly dark sky has a surface brightness of 2×10−4 cd m−2 or 21.8 mag arcsec−2. The peak surface brightness of the central region of the Orion Nebula is about 17 Mag/arcsec2 (about 14 millinits) and the outer bluish glow has a peak surface brightness of 21.3 Mag/arcsec2 (about 0.27 millinits).

Pixel scale describes how much of the sky falls on a single pixel of the camera sensor. It is given in arcseconds per pixel and follows from two values: the physical pixel size of the camera and the effective focal length of the telescope, including any reducer or Barlow lens. The usual formula is pixel scale = 206.265 × pixel size in micrometres / focal length in millimetres. A camera with 3.76 µm pixels behind a telescope with 550 mm focal length, for example, records about 1.4 arcseconds per pixel. The constant 206.265 converts the ratio of micrometres to millimetres into arcseconds.

The field of view of a camera follows from the same quantities: the sensor size in millimetres divided by the focal length gives the angle the sensor covers on the sky. A short focal length and a large sensor give a wide field for large nebulae and Milky Way regions; a long focal length gives a narrow field for small galaxies and planetary nebulae. Pixel scale and field of view are therefore two views of the same choice of telescope and camera.

Sampling compares the pixel scale with the finest detail the sky allows. Under typical seeing the image of a star is blurred to a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of about 2 to 4 arcseconds. A common rule of thumb, derived from the Nyquist criterion, is to place two to three pixels across the FWHM of a star. With a FWHM of 3 arcseconds this suggests a pixel scale between about 1 and 1.5 arcseconds per pixel.

An image is undersampled when the pixels are too large compared with the seeing, for example 3 to 4 arcseconds per pixel under good seeing. Stars become small and blocky, sometimes square, and fine detail is lost. Undersampling is common with short focal lengths and is acceptable for wide fields. Dithering and drizzle integration can recover part of the lost resolution when many frames are stacked.

An image is oversampled when the pixels are much smaller than the seeing disc, for example 0.3 arcseconds per pixel under 3 arcseconds of seeing. The image shows no more detail, but the light of a star or nebula is spread over more pixels, so every pixel collects less signal and the signal-to-noise ratio per pixel drops. Oversampled data can be binned, either in the camera or in software, to combine neighbouring pixels and bring the pixel scale closer to the seeing.

For the planets and the Moon the rules differ. Lucky imaging uses very short exposures to freeze moments of good seeing, so the useful resolution is limited by the aperture of the telescope rather than by the average seeing. Planetary imagers therefore choose a much finer pixel scale and often a focal ratio of about five times the pixel size in micrometres, reached with a Barlow lens.

Pixel scale is fixed by the equipment, while seeing changes from night to night. A setup that samples well on an average night is a good compromise. Tools that plan an imaging session should calculate pixel scale and field of view from the actual telescope and camera instead of relying on rules of thumb, and should report whether a target fits the field.

Colour images of deep-sky objects are usually assembled from several monochrome exposures taken through different filters. The way these channels are mapped to the red, green and blue channels of the final image is called a palette. The most common schemes are LRGB for broadband targets and HOO and SHO for narrowband targets.

LRGB combines a luminance channel (L) with red, green and blue channels. The luminance filter passes the whole visible spectrum and collects most of the signal, so it carries the detail and the signal-to-noise ratio of the image. The red, green and blue filters provide the colour information and can be shorter or binned. LRGB suits targets that emit a continuous spectrum: galaxies, star clusters, reflection nebulae and dark nebulae. Its weakness is light pollution and moonlight, which are also broadband and reduce contrast. A one-shot colour camera records the RGB part in a single exposure through its Bayer matrix.

Emission nebulae shine in a few spectral lines. The most important for imaging are hydrogen-alpha (Ha) at 656.3 nm, doubly ionized oxygen (OIII) at 495.9 and 500.7 nm, and singly ionized sulphur (SII) at 671.6 nm. Narrowband filters pass only a few nanometres around these lines. They block most light pollution and moonlight, which makes narrowband imaging possible from cities and on moonlit nights.

HOO uses two filters: Ha is mapped to red, and OIII is mapped to both green and blue. The result resembles the natural colours of many emission nebulae, with red hydrogen regions and teal oxygen regions. HOO needs only two filters and is popular with dual-band filters on colour cameras, which pass Ha and OIII at the same time. It works well for planetary nebulae, supernova remnants and nebulae with strong oxygen emission.

SHO, also called the Hubble palette, maps SII to red, Ha to green and OIII to blue. Because hydrogen usually dominates, raw SHO images look green; processing shifts the hues so that hydrogen appears golden and oxygen blue. SHO separates regions of different ionization and shows structure that HOO hides, at the cost of a third filter and long exposures for the often faint SII signal. It is a false-colour palette: the colours encode chemistry rather than what the eye would see.

Broadband targets such as galaxies call for LRGB or RGB. Emission nebulae call for narrowband: HOO when two filters are available or oxygen is strong, SHO when sulphur emission is present and three filters are available. Many images combine both, for example RGB stars with narrowband nebulosity, or Ha added to the red channel of an RGB galaxy to show its star-forming regions.

Dithering means moving the telescope by a small, random amount between individual exposures, so that the target falls on slightly different pixels in every frame. Typical shifts are a few to a few dozen pixels. The images are registered on the stars before stacking, so the target lines up again, while every defect of the sensor ends up at a different position on the sky.

Camera sensors have fixed patterns: hot pixels, cold pixels, column defects and a faint pattern of amplifier glow and read noise. Calibration frames remove most of these, but not all. Without dithering the residual pattern stays at the same place in every frame and survives stacking; it often shows up as coloured streaks, so-called walking noise, when the guiding drifts slowly in one direction. With dithering the residual pattern is spread over different positions, and statistical rejection during stacking, for example sigma clipping, removes it like any other outlier.

A shift of a few times the size of a star image is usually enough. Many imagers dither after every frame or every few frames. Each dither costs some seconds of settling time for the mount and the guiding, so very short exposures make frequent dithering expensive; then dithering every few frames is a reasonable compromise. Dithering needs a guided mount or a mount control program that can move the telescope between frames.

Drizzle integration combines many slightly shifted frames onto a finer output grid. It can recover resolution from undersampled data, but only if the frames are shifted by fractions of a pixel. Dithering provides exactly these shifts, so drizzle and dithering are normally used together.
Lucky imaging of the planets and the Moon uses thousands of very short frames in a video. Natural seeing and small tracking errors already shift the image, so explicit dithering is not used there.

Calibration frames are exposures that record the unwanted signal of the camera and the optical system, so that it can be removed from the light frames that contain the target. The usual set consists of bias, dark, flat and dark-flat frames. They are taken with the same camera and, where it matters, with the same settings as the light frames.

A bias frame is the shortest possible exposure with the shutter closed or the telescope covered. It records the offset that the camera adds to every pixel and the pattern of the readout electronics. Many bias frames are averaged into a master bias. With modern CMOS cameras bias frames are sometimes replaced by dark-flat frames, because very short exposures can behave differently from longer ones.

A dark frame is an exposure with the same exposure time, gain and sensor temperature as the light frames, but without light. It records the thermal signal (dark current), hot pixels and amplifier glow. Subtracting a master dark removes this signal from the light frames. Cooled cameras make darks reusable, because the sensor temperature can be held constant; uncooled cameras need darks taken under similar conditions.

A flat frame is an exposure of an evenly illuminated surface, for example a light panel or the twilight sky, through the same optical train, focus position and filter as the light frames. It records vignetting, dust shadows (so-called dust donuts) and differences in pixel sensitivity. Dividing the light frames by a normalized master flat corrects these effects. Flats must be taken for every filter and whenever the camera rotation or focus changes. A good flat exposure reaches roughly a third to a half of the full well.

Dark-flat frames have the same exposure time as the flats but no light. They remove the offset and dark signal from the flats before the flats are used, and they replace bias frames with many CMOS cameras.

A calibrated light frame is calculated as (light − master dark) / (master flat − master dark-flat), with the flat normalized to an average of one. Stacking software applies these steps automatically before registration and integration. Calibration does not add signal; it removes systematic errors, so that the noise in the final image is mainly the random noise of the light frames.

A deep-sky image is not taken as one long exposure. It is built from many single exposures, called sub-exposures or subs, which are calibrated, aligned and stacked. The sum of all sub-exposure times is the integration time. Integration time decides how deep and clean the final image is; the length of a single sub is a separate choice.

Noise in astronomical images is mostly random: photon shot noise of the target and the sky, read noise of the camera and thermal noise. When frames are stacked, the signal grows with the number of frames while random noise grows only with its square root. The signal-to-noise ratio therefore improves with the square root of the integration time: four times the integration time halves the relative noise. Faint nebulae and the outer regions of galaxies need many hours, while bright objects need far less.

A single sub should be long enough that the camera's read noise becomes small compared with the shot noise of the sky background; beyond that point longer subs add little. Under bright, light-polluted skies or with broadband filters this point is reached after short exposures, often well under a minute with modern CMOS cameras. Narrowband filters block most of the sky background, so narrowband subs are usually several minutes long. Very long subs carry risks: saturated stars, lost frames through clouds, satellites or wind, and tracking errors.

CMOS cameras let the user choose gain and offset. A higher gain lowers read noise but reduces the full well, so bright stars saturate earlier. Many imagers use the gain at which the camera switches to its low-noise mode. The offset must be high enough that no pixel is clipped to zero in a bias or dark frame.

An imaging plan distributes the available time of a night over the filters. Broadband LRGB often spends more time on luminance; narrowband plans give the faint OIII or SII channels more time than the bright Ha channel. The usable time is limited by the period in which the target is high enough and the sky dark enough. Splitting a project over several nights is common, and every night adds to the integration of the same target.

Planetary and lunar imaging work differently: thousands of very short frames are recorded as a video within a few minutes, before the rotation of the planet blurs the details. Only the sharpest frames are kept and stacked.
Astronomy cameras come in two kinds: monochrome cameras and one-shot colour (OSC) cameras. Both use the same kinds of sensors; the difference is a colour filter array on the sensor of the OSC camera.

An OSC camera has a Bayer matrix of tiny red, green and blue filters in front of its pixels, usually in a pattern with two green pixels for every red and blue one. Each pixel records only one colour, and software reconstructs a full colour image by debayering. An OSC camera produces a colour image in a single exposure, needs no filter wheel and keeps the imaging session simple. Because every pixel loses about two thirds of the light to its colour filter, an OSC camera collects colour information more slowly than a monochrome camera with a full set of filters, and its effective resolution per colour is lower.

A monochrome camera records all light that reaches each pixel. Colour comes from separate exposures through filters in a filter wheel: L, R, G and B for broadband images, or Ha, OIII and SII for narrowband images. Every pixel is used for every filter, so mono cameras reach a given signal-to-noise ratio faster, especially in narrowband, where each line can be imaged through a dedicated filter. The cost is more equipment, more calibration frames (flats for each filter) and longer projects across several nights.

Dual-band and tri-band filters pass several emission lines at once and make narrowband imaging possible with OSC cameras. Ha falls on the red pixels and OIII mainly on the green and blue pixels, so a HOO image can be extracted from one set of exposures. This is efficient but cannot match the separation and depth of dedicated narrowband filters on a monochrome camera.

OSC cameras suit beginners, short sessions, broadband targets and imaging from dark sites. Monochrome cameras suit narrowband imaging from light-polluted locations and imagers who want the highest efficiency and flexibility. For planetary imaging both are used; colour cameras are common because they record all colours in one video while the planet rotates.
